item1_text: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of Canada introduced emergency benefits to support Canadians by providing temporary income support for workers (employed and self-employed) who were directly impacted by the pandemic. These emergency benefits are: Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Federal emergency benefits received in 2020 are considered income for the 2021-2022 payment period. Clients who received EI-ERB and saw a reduction of their income-tested benefits during the 2021-2022 payment period might have qualified for an option when the emergency benefit ended. Effective July 2022, these benefits are no longer considered income when calculating entitlement to income-tested benefits. For more information about these benefits and how this income was reported to the Department by the CRA , refer to: Calculating Income (Policy) ; and Calculating Income (Policy) COVID-19: Interim Measures—Emergency Benefits (Action) . item2_text: As part of the COVID-19 Emergency Response Act, the Government of Canada introduced the Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act (CERB Act) that paid income support to eligible Canadians and was administered through the CRA. In order to provide similar support for workers who would generally be eligible for the EI program, the Minister made interim orders providing for the EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) administered by Service Canada . Although the CRA and Service Canada jointly administered the Emergency Response Benefits, existing EI processes as well as two different pieces of legislation have led to some differences in how the benefits were administered depending on which Department an individual applied through. Subsection 153.121(1) of the EIA states: 153.121 (1) A benefit period that was established for a claimant before March 15, 2020 — including a benefit period established in respect of benefits payable under Part VIII — ends the day before the first week for which the claimant is paid an employment insurance emergency response benefit. This section of the legislation required claimants who had an existing EI claim to terminate that EI claim if they wished to receive the EI ERB on or after March 15, 2020. Once an EI claim is terminated, the hours and earnings used to establish that claim cannot be used again and claimants lose any remaining entitlement weeks on that claim. However, there is no corresponding piece of legislation in the CERB Act. Part VIII.4 of the EIA applies only to the EI ERB, it cannot be used to support decisions made on CERB claims paid by the CRA. As a result, if claimants had an existing EI claim and then chose to collect the CERB through the CRA, their existing EI claim was not terminated and these claimants may now come back to collect EI and have their earlier claims renewed. There is nothing to legally prevent claimants from renewing their previous EI claim following the payment of CERB through the CRA provided that they are not renewing it for a period where they were in receipt of CERB payments. It is important to note, however, that renewing the claim may not be to the claimant’s advantage. Any EI claim with a BPC prior to September 27, 2020 will not benefit from the temporary transition measures (including the minimum benefit rate). If a claimant wishes to terminate their earlier claim to avail of the temporary transition measures, the usual procedures for terminating an EI claim must be followed. Example

item1_text: When you determine that a payment should not be delivered to a payee, you can access the SPS and intercept it. This prevents the issuing of a payment. The intercepted payment can be cancelled, remailed or reissued to the payee, if applicable. Previously, the same user had the delegated authority to intercept a payment, modify the payment destination and reissue the same payment. Since October 26, 2017, SPS does not allow you to intercept and redirect the same payment. The additional security measure allows you to: intercept a payment and have another user modify the payment destination or reissue the payment; and modify a payment destination or reissue a payment after a payment has been intercepted by another user. This additional security measure is similar to the current segregation of duties for inputting and authorizing a priority payment. For more information, refer to the Delegation of Authorities (PDF, 313 KB) Download link . Delegation of Authorities There is a limited timeframe to intercept a payment after it is loaded into the SPS and before it is extracted. The payment must have a Payment Status of Ready for Extract . The OAS benefit payment date is the same for every region, but the schedule of production of payments may vary by region. You will follow the production schedule to obtain specific information on when CPP and OAS payments are loaded into the SPS and the final intercept dates. To view current and past production schedules, refer to the Benefits Toolbox . In some cases, you may need to keep track of or hold a file until the payment appears in SPS and is ready for extract. Benefits Toolbox Intercepting payments reduces the need to pull cheques or recall direct deposit payments after the extract date. In emergency situations, such as when a payment is determined to be fraudulent or when issuing a payment will result in a substantial overpayment, cheque pulls and direct deposit recalls may still be requested. If a new address or new banking information is required to issue a payment, and SPS shows the Payment Status as Ready for Extract , this must be actioned immediately. SPS only allows a payment to be reissued the same day it has been intercepted. If you intercept a payment without reissuing it the same day, SPS will extract the payment and cancel it automatically. SPS will update the payment with the return reason Intercepted at the extract date .

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the criteria for processing reconsideration requests received after a specified time limit, but they present different time frames and criteria for assessing these requests. Passage 1 focuses on a 90-day and 365-day framework, while Passage 2 introduces a 30-day threshold and categorizes delays into short and longer delays, leading to conflicting interpretations of the timelines and requirements for reconsideration requests.
item1_article_title: Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit
item2_article_title: Processing a delayed request for reconsideration
item1_text: The CPP and OAS regulations set out the criteria to be used for assessing a request for an extension of the 90-day time limit: within 365 days of the notification of the initial decision; and beyond 365 days following the notification of the initial decision. Reconsideration request received beyond the 90-day time limit but within 365 days If a request for reconsideration is received outside of the 90-day time limit but within 365 days of notification of the initial decision, the Minister’s delegate must assess the following 2 criteria: Is there a reasonable explanation for the delay? and Was there a continuing intention to request the reconsideration? Criterion 1—There is a reasonable explanation for the delay A reasonable explanation for the delay in requesting a reconsideration exists if there are exceptional or extenuating circumstances. Exceptional circumstances include information that relates to an applicant's or beneficiaries medical condition that prevents them from acting with reasonable diligence. Extenuating circumstances are related to situational factors that are unusual, unexpected or unavoidable and beyond the applicant's or beneficiary’s control and which have prevented them from submitting a timely request. Criterion 2—There is a continuing intention Continuing intention to request a reconsideration exists if the available information indicates the applicant or beneficiary had the intent to request a reconsideration during the 90-day time period. In some cases, there is an interaction between exceptional or extenuating circumstances and the demonstration of continuing intention, which should be taken into consideration when assessing the request. Reconsideration request is received beyond 365 days When a request for reconsideration is received beyond 365 days following the notification of the initial decision, the Minister’s delegate must assess the following 4 criteria: Is there a reasonable explanation for the delay in requesting a reconsideration? Was there a continuing intention to request a reconsideration ? If the request for reconsideration has a reasonable chance of success; and If the extension would cause prejudice to the Minister or another party. Criterion 3—A request for reconsideration has a reasonable chance of success A reasonable chance of success exists when the decision to deny a benefit or provision is disputable, debatable or open to question. Generally, for the purposes of considering whether the applicant or beneficiary has a reasonable chance of success in the context of an extension of the reconsideration 90-day time limit, the applicant or beneficiary must provide evidence to support their reconsideration request that was not presented to the initial decision-maker. If no new information is provided or no reasons are given to explain why the initial decision was incorrect, there is no reasonable chance of success for the reconsideration. Criterion 4—No prejudice would be caused to the Minister or another party by allowing a longer period to make the request In the majority of cases, it is not likely that unfairness to the Minister will be a significant factor in determining whether to allow the extension. Prejudice, or unfairness, can occur due to a time lapse of months or years. It can also be determined that there is a prejudice to the Minister or another party in situations where a file has been destroyed according to departmental file management guidelines. In these cases, the Minister may no longer have pertinent evidence available to reconsider the facts, which were present when the initial decision was made.
item2_text: A request made more than 30 days after the date on which a notice of decision is received is considered a delayed request. However, the request can still be accepted if a reasonable explanation for the delay is provided. Processing a short delay Delays that do not exceed 120 days after the initial decision are considered short delays and are allowed without further fact-finding or documentation. The short delay period is considered a reasonable explanation in itself. Processing a request received between 121 and 365 days after the initial decision For delays between 121 and 365 days after the initial decision, requesters must provide a reasonable explanation for the delay and demonstrate a continued intention to request a reconsideration under EIA 112 . Each argument provided to explain the delay must be assessed individually. EIA 112 Note Processing a request received beyond 365 days and in other particular circumstances The following 3 circumstances require special consideration: More than 365 days have passed since the decision was communicated to the requester. The requester submitted another application for benefits after the decision was communicated. The requester has asked the Commission to rescind or amend the decision under EIA 111 . EIA 111 If any of these circumstances are present, the officer must first determine if the requester provided a reasonable explanation for the delay and demonstrated a continued intention to request a reconsideration under EIA 112. If these 2 conditions are not met, the delay can be denied. However, if these 2 conditions are met, the Commission must also be satisfied that the request for reconsideration on the substantive issue has a reasonable chance of success and that no prejudice would be caused to the Commission or any other interested party.

item1_text: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of Canada introduced emergency benefits to support Canadians by providing temporary income support for workers (employed and self-employed) who were directly impacted by the pandemic. These emergency benefits are: Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Clients who received EI-ERB and saw a reduction of their income-tested benefits during the 2021-2022 payment period might have qualified for an option when the emergency benefit ended. item2_text: Info The CERB and the EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) were important and necessary temporary responses to support Canadians who had to stop working due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The eligibility requirement stating that a self-employed person must have an income of at least $5 000 (in 2019 or in the last 12 months) to receive the CERB or EI ERB was always considered as the net pre-tax income (i.e. gross income less expenses). On February 9, 2021, the Government of Canada announced that self-employed workerswhose net self-employment (SE) income was less than $5 000 and who applied for the CERB do not have to repay the CERB or the EI ERB, as long as their gross SE income was at least $5 000 and they met all other eligibility criteria. Some self-employed workers whose net SE earnings were less than $5 000 may have already voluntarily repaid the CERB or the EI ERB. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Service Canada will return the repaid amounts to the impacted persons. Today, the Government of Canada announced further details about the reimbursement process. Self-employed workers whose net SE income was less than $5 000 and who applied for the CERB or the EI ERB are not required to repay these benefits, as long as they meet all of the following criteria: They have filed their 2019 and 2020 income tax returns before December 31, 2022. They applied for the CERB or the EI ERB based on their SE income. Their gross SE income was $5 000 or more. They met all other CERB eligibility criteria. The CRA will review the 2019 and 2020 income tax returns of self-employed workers in this situation to verify that they: earned $5 000 or more in gross SE income in either year (or in the 12 months before their initial application); met all other CERB eligibility criteria. Starting on May 27, 2021, self-employed workers who meet these criteria and who had voluntarily repaid either the CRA or Service Canada all or part of the CERB or EI ERB in 2020 can request a reimbursement. To do so, they must complete the CERB Reimbursement Application for Self-Employed Individuals formand submit it to the CRA electronically or by mail . CERB Reimbursement Application for Self-Employed Individuals Workers who repaid the CERB can expect reimbursements within approximately 90 calendar days of submitting their application to the CRA.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the calculation of penalty amounts for misrepresentation, but they provide different methods and percentages for determining these penalties. Passage 1 states that the penalty for a first misrepresentation is based on 10% of the accumulated overpayment or 10% of the maximum monthly benefit rate, while Passage 2 states that the penalty for a first misrepresentation can be up to 50% of the net overpayment to a maximum of $5,000. Additionally, the maximum penalty amounts and the conditions for subsequent misrepresentations differ between the two passages, leading to conflicting information regarding how penalties are calculated.
item1_text: When the Integrity Services Branch determines that a misrepresentation was knowingly made and makes a recommendation to apply a penalty, determine the penalty amount to be imposed. To determine the penalty amount, consider the following: The maximum legislated penalty allowed for each misrepresentation is $10,000. In a first misrepresentation, the penalty is based on an amount not more than 10% of the accumulated overpayment or, if there is no overpayment, on an amount not more than 10% of the maximum monthly benefit rate for that program. In a subsequent misrepresentation, the penalty amount is based on an amount not more than 20% of the accumulated overpayment or, if there is no overpayment, on an amount not more than 20% of the maximum monthly benefit rate for that program. To determine whether a misrepresentation should be penalized as a first or subsequent misrepresentation , the Minister must be aware of the subsequent misrepresentation and it must be within 10 years from the date a previous penalty was imposed. The penalty amount may be reduced depending on an individual’s mitigating circumstances, outlined in the Report of Investigation. Mitigating circumstances determined to be valid may allow the penalty amount to be reduced by any percentage up to 100%. The minimum penalty amount is $0.00. A $0.00 amount still counts as a penalty. This is an important consideration when establishing a subsequent misrepresentation.
item2_text: A penalty is a monetary sanction that can be imposed on clients who have knowingly made false statements (i.e. misrepresentative). The penalty amount is calculated as a percentage of the net OP amount for weeks within the reconsideration timeframe: penalty amount = net OP × penalty percentage. The net OP is the dollar value obtained by adding all OPs and subtracting all UPs resulting from the misrepresentation. Only the net OP established within the 36-month limitation period is used to calculate the penalty amount. A penalty amount is rounded up to the next dollar (for values of .50 and greater) and always established for the current tax year. When calculating the penalty amount, the officer takes into account the following elements: net OP amount maximum penalty amount per BPC level of misrepresentation legal validation amount The maximum penalty amount increases when a subsequent act of misrepresentation follows the notification of previous misrepresentation. A second level misrepresentation (e.g. repetitive misrepresentation) that occurs within 260 weeks of the notification of a previous misrepresentation is a second level misrepresentation. The levels of misrepresentation and corresponding penalty caps are as follows: First misrepresentation: Up to 50% of the net OP to a maximum of $5 000 per BPC. Second misrepresentation: Up to 100% of the net OP to a maximum of $8 000 per BPC. Third or more misrepresentation: Up to 150% of the net OP to a maximum of $10 000 per BPC. If some weeks were processed before a first level of misrepresentation and some weeks were processed after, the penalty is calculated as follows: 50% of the new OP for the weeks that were processed before the previous notification week; 100% of the new OP for weeks that were processed after. In addition to the levels of misrepresentation and maximums, the penalty amount cannot exceed the legal validation amount . The legal validation amount is calculated as follows: 3 x the benefit rate x number of false statements = maximum penalty amount. The number of false statements corresponds to the number of claimant’s reports for which the client provided false information. One claimant’s report is one false statement even when there are multiple omissions or errors on the same report. final_analysis: Both passages describe the assistance measure in Quebec, detailing the role of assistants, the verification process through the Public register of assistants, and the requirements for identification. item1_text: The assistance measure allows a person experiencing a difficulty to be assisted free of charge by one or two people of their choice. Officially recognized by the Curateur public du Québec, the assistant can then communicate with third parties (government services, financial institutions, businesses, service providers and professionals) on behalf of the assisted person. Assistants cannot sign or make decisions on behalf of applicants or clients. As an authorized contact, their scope is limited to communication. The authority of an assistant is similar to the authority granted to an individual through a Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP-1603) form. Duration and termination The assistant is recognized for a maximum period of 3 years. After this period, a new application must be submitted to have the same person or up to 2 new persons recognized for an additional 3-year period. However, the assistance measure can be terminated at any time before the end of the three years in any of the following situations: at the request of the assisted person; when the Curateur public du Québec is informed that the assistant ceases to act; upon the death of the assisted person or the assistant; upon institution of a tutorship for the assisted person or for their assistant; following the homologation of the assisted person's or the assistant's protection mandate; following the appointment of a temporary representative for the assistant; or when the Curateur public du Québec decides to terminate it. Verification Assistants recognized by the Curateur public du Québec are officially registered in the Public register of assistants. You must consult the Public register of assistants whenever an assistant comes forward to communicate on behalf of the client. This register allows you to verify the identity of any assistant when they contact you to obtain information on behalf of the assisted person. Consulting the Public register of assistants is the only way to verify if an assistant is registered and if their recognition is still valid. To access the Public register of assistants, you will need the first and last name of the assistant and the measure number that the assistant will provide. The assistant will also be required to obtain and provide you with a security code. This code is valid for 72 hours and will allow you to see the identity (first and last name) of the assisted person. To verify the identity of an assistant when they contact you, refer to Public register of assistants External link . Public register of assistants
item2_text: Quebec — Assistance measure The assistance measure is a program in the province of Quebec that allows registered assistants that are officially recognized by the Curateur public to obtain the same information for a client as other authorized third parties. To verify if assistants are registered, officers refer to the Public register of assistants . The information on the page is available in both official languages. However, the page to verify the registration of an assistant is only available in French. If necessary, the officer changes the WI to bilingual and reassigns it to the next available user. Assistants must provide their first and last name and the measure number for identification purposes. They must also provide a security code that is only valid for 72 hours and which is used to identify the first and last name of the assisted person. Being a registered assistant under the assistance measure in the province of Quebec is not the equivalent of being a representative as per the INS3280 form. assistance measure Public register of assistants

item1_text: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of Canada introduced emergency benefits to support Canadians by providing temporary income support for workers (employed and self-employed) who were directly impacted by the pandemic. These emergency benefits are: Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). item2_article_title: Reasons for a returned direct deposit payment
item1_text: Payments are commonly returned for one of the following reasons: The payee's entitlement ceases (e.g. a beneficiary dies, a survivor receiving OAS benefits remarries, a surviving child receiving CPP benefits who is over the age of 18 and leaves school). The payee died, and the estate cannot cash the payment as it was originally issued to the client. There is a change of payee (e.g. a trustee dies). The payee's address changed or the payee cannot be located. The payee's name changed (e.g. the payee marries or remarries). The payee's name is incorrect. The payee's bank account number changed. The payee's bank account is closed, frozen or transferred to another financial institution. The payee receives an original payment and its duplicate one and returns one of the two payments; The bank deems a cheque to be stale-dated. The Department stops or recalls a payment. The client requests to have their benefit cancelled. The Imaging and Receiver General Operations Directorate records all returned payments in SPS. The Payment Information Status indicates Outstanding and the Payment Attempt Status indicates Returned with a return Reason Code .
item2_text: The following are the most common reasons for a returned direct deposit payment, displayed in the Payment Attempt Status section in SPS: Payee deceased When a payment is returned because the client is deceased, the IPOC officer refers the case to a processing officer. Incorrect payee name Banks can refuse to deposit a payment when the payee name is different than the client’s current name on the account that applies. Payments requiring a payee name change cannot be replaced. Instead, they must be cancelled and reissued. The IPOC officer refers the file to a processing officer. Customer initiated return Clients may refuse a payment because they are not entitled to the payment or would like it applied to an outstanding overpayment (OP). This requires a payment cancellation. The IPOC officer refers the file to a processing officer. Auto pulled SPS prevents a direct deposit payment from being issued to a bank account when 3 previous direct deposit payments were rejected for the same account. This is called an autopull. SPS automatically pulls any payments destined for the account until the client’s direct deposit information is verified. The IPOC officer confirms the direct deposit information with the client and replaces the payment. SPS automatically removes the autopull when the payment is replaced. They provide similar information about the need to review circumstances and their impact on penalty amounts, despite some differences in wording and specific details.
item1_text: Once it is determined that an individual has knowingly misrepresented, mitigating circumstances must be considered. Mitigating circumstances are situations, facts or actions that can offer some explanation of the individual's actions and lead to a possible reduction of the penalty amount. Although these circumstances offer some explanation, they do not excuse the misrepresentation. The Integrity Services Branch (ISB) will investigate the information surrounding these mitigating circumstances and will clearly document them in their Report of Investigation (ROI). The ISB will not take mitigating circumstances into consideration when making a recommendation to impose a penalty. However, you must consider the mitigating circumstances when determining the penalty amount. For more information, refer to Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) and Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) Assessing Mitigating Circumstances (Action)
item2_text: The Level 2 agent must review all documents, facts and information on file to determine whether there are mitigating circumstances that could reduce the sanction for the misrepresentation. The existence of mitigating circumstances must never be assumed. There must be a clear indication that such circumstances exist. Mitigating circumstances usually relate to the time when the misrepresentation occurred, but there are some that may exist up to and including the time the case is being reviewed by an adjudicator or even after the decision has been reached. A percentage value is assigned to the mitigating circumstances. When calculating the penalty amount, the maximum penalty amount based on the level of misrepresentation is reduced by the percentage value of the mitigating circumstances.

final_analysis: Both passages describe the assistance measure in Quebec, detailing the role and limitations of assistants, the process of registration with the Curateur public, and the verification through the Public register of assistants. item1_text: The assistance measure allows a person experiencing a difficulty to be assisted free of charge by one or two people of their choice. Officially recognized by the Curateur public du Québec, the assistant can then communicate with third parties (government services, financial institutions, businesses, service providers and professionals) on behalf of the assisted person. Assistants cannot sign or make decisions on behalf of applicants or clients. As an authorized contact, their scope is limited to communication. The authority of an assistant is similar to the authority granted to an individual through a Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP-1603) form. Duration and termination The assistant is recognized for a maximum period of 3 years. After this period, a new application must be submitted to have the same person or up to 2 new persons recognized for an additional 3-year period. However, the assistance measure can be terminated at any time before the end of the three years in any of the following situations: at the request of the assisted person; when the Curateur public du Québec is informed that the assistant ceases to act; upon the death of the assisted person or the assistant; upon institution of a tutorship for the assisted person or for their assistant; following the homologation of the assisted person's or the assistant's protection mandate; following the appointment of a temporary representative for the assistant; or when the Curateur public du Québec decides to terminate it. Verification Assistants recognized by the Curateur public du Québec are officially registered in the Public register of assistants. You must consult the Public register of assistants whenever an assistant comes forward to communicate on behalf of the client. This register allows you to verify the identity of any assistant when they contact you to obtain information on behalf of the assisted person. Consulting the Public register of assistants is the only way to verify if an assistant is registered and if their recognition is still valid. To access the Public register of assistants, you will need the first and last name of the assistant and the measure number that the assistant will provide. The assistant will also be required to obtain and provide you with a security code. This code is valid for 72 hours and will allow you to see the identity (first and last name) of the assisted person. To verify the identity of an assistant when they contact you, refer to Public register of assistants External link . Public register of assistants
item2_text: The assistance measure in the province of Quebec is a program that allows a client to designate an individual as a registered assistant. The client submits an application directly to the Curateur public, which allows the assistant’s name to appear in the Public register of assistants. The registered assistant can obtain third party information in the same way as an individual authorized by the client with the Access to information: INS3124 Individual’s consent to disclosure or use — Form. Using the Public register of assistants, the officer validates the official recognition of the assistant. Being an approved assistant is not the equivalent of being a representative under the Representative: INS3280 Appointment — Form, but rather, it means being an authorized third party. Related tasks in the EI ORT have been updated to reflect this new regional consideration for the province of Quebec.

item1_text: Clients can submit a request for reconsideration anytime they disagree with a decision made on their case. The client must submit a request for reconsideration within 90 days of the date of the decision letter from Service Canada. The request for reconsideration can be submitted using the Request for Reconsideration of an Old Age Security Decision (ISP-3134) form or online through the client portal. When a client submits a request for reconsideration from the client portal, a request for reconsideration task is created in the appropriate work queue. Cúram automatically displays a corresponding reconsideration flag on the context panel for the Person or Prospect Person and associated case for the client. When a written request for reconsideration is processed, a task is created in Cúram that shows the client's SIN or Cúram Reference Number, the client's name, and Request for Reconsideration for the Type. The request is also listed as an attachment under the Contacts tab. You must manually add a flag to the client's profile to indicate it is under reconsideration. When the reconsideration is closed, you must remove the flag. When there is a reconsideration on an account with an overpayment that resulted from the decision the client is requesting the reconsideration for, recovery action must be deferred if it has not been initiated. If recovery has already been initiated, then it must be suspended until the outcome of the reconsideration, or the appeal is known. You should manually de-activate a payment correction or overpayment (manual) case deduction for a departmental liability.
item2_text: Explain the right to submit a request for reconsideration and define the appropriate time frames: If the claim is not established at the time of the verbal communication, advise the client to wait until he or she has received the notice of decision before submitting a request for reconsideration. item1_article_title: Redirect or reissue a payment in SPS
item1_text: To redirect or reissue a payment that has been intercepted, proceed as follows: Access SPS. Refer to the Standard Payment System user guide External link . Standard Payment System user guide Under Main Menu select Regular Payment Processing and under Screen select Correct Input Errors . Enter the 12-digit number of the Payment Reference Number and click GO . To complete this action, the Payment Attempt Status must be Ready for Extract or Awaiting Correction . Enter the correct address and postal code, banking information or payment amount, click SUBMIT . To confirm the action, click CONFIRM . To cancel the action, click CANCEL .
item2_text: A request to reissue a payment can be received at the same time as the request for cancellation (i.e. on the same MM06) or after the cancellation process has been started. Once a payment has been cancelled, all information related to that payment is removed. This is why a cancelled payment cannot be replaced in SPS. It must be reissued as a new payment. item1_text: Action the request for reconsideration of the imposition of an administrative penalty or the penalty amount.
item2_text: The agent imposes an administrative penalty (monetary or warning letter) if a client makes a misrepresentation for which neither the voluntary disclosure policy nor prosecution is applicable. A violation must be considered whenever a sanction (monetary or non-monetary) has been imposed. A client who is subject to a penalty or violation may provide additional information that could lead to a reconsideration of the decision. The client can also ask for an administrative review of a claim decision. EIA 41 gives the Commission authority to remove or reduce a penalty or to remove a violation. Once the inputs are completed the agent returns to the originating task to complete the remainder of the steps required (e.g. to send a letter). This procedure also applies to decisions made through the EIA 112 or EIA 52 reconsideration process. item1_article_title: Leave a message on a voicemail or with a third party
item1_text: If you are calling the client or their authorized representative, you must leave a message on a voicemail service when there is no answer. You are not required to confirm that the voicemail includes the client's or their authorized representative's name before leaving a voicemail requesting a call back. If an unauthorized third party answers the client's or the authorized representative's phone, you can leave a message with that individual. Leave a message on the voicemail or with the third party with the following details. For script examples, refer to Call Scripts for Client Engagement : Identify yourself including your name and that you are calling from Service Canada; Indicate who the message is for; Ask for the client or their authorized representative to call you back; Provide one of the following numbers: your direct phone number including the area code if it is necessary to speak with the client or their authorized representative regarding the client's file. one of the following Service Canada Call Centre numbers if the call is general in nature: 1-800-277-9914 (English) 1-800-277-9915 (French) 1-800-255-4786—Teletype users 1-800-454-8731—International Operations 1-613-957-1954 (collect calls will be accepted) 1-800-255-4786—Teletype users Call Scripts for Client Engagement Update ITRDS notes and complete the Telephone Call (ISP-0112) form or the applicable CPPD form to record: the date and time of the call; the reason for the call; that a message was left requesting a call-back; and your name and direct phone number for call centre staff to redirect the client's call, if applicable.
